To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(i) the glycosome is permeable to all glycolytic metabolites, and (ii) the glycosomal compartmentalization of glycolysis is not essential for the survival of the parasite.
(1) the glycosomal pores are not incompatible with our current understanding of glycolysis, and (2) the glycosomes are not as compartmentalized as previously assumed.

(i) a model of glycolytic metabolism in T. brucci is consistent with the existence of size‐specific pores in the glycosome membrane, (ii) these pores are not necessarily inconsistent with the current knowledge of the metabolic system of the glycosome and (iii) the existence of these pores does not affect the conclusion that the glycosomal compartment is important for the regulation of the fluxes in the glycolytic network of T. brucci.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a new model of the glycolysis in T. brucci and with the question of how the topology of the model can be determined.
the question of how much information about a biological system is needed to be able to make predictions about its function.
the question of how the topology of metabolic pathways can be inferred from the available experimental data.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the glycosomal system is neither completely impermeable, nor is it a freely permeable system.
the glycosome is indeed an important compartment of T. bruceis metabolism, but it is not a strictly impermeable compartment as previously believed.
the topology of the glycosome is not yet fully understood and that the role of the newly‐discovered channels in the regulation of the glycolysis is not yet fully established.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the new finding about the permeability of the glycosome is not in contradiction with the current model of the glycosomes in T. brusei.

the newly discovered nonspecific pores in glycosomal membranes are not necessarily incompatible either with the current knowledge of the metabolic system of T. bruce in glycosomes or with the current knowledge about glycolytic flux and the concentrations of metabolic intermediates.

the glycosomal system in T. brucei can be described by a metabolic network that is not necessarily compartmentalized, but rather by a network of interconnected compartments that are linked by specific transporters.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the topology of the glycolysis in T. bracei can be considered as an additional parameter of the system.

the new findings about the permeability of the glycosome membrane do not necessarily contradict the assumption that the glycosome is the site of most of the glycosyltransferases in the T. bruceibody, but rather suggest a more complex picture of the metabolic system.

the new findings on the topology of glycosomes can be reconciled with the existing knowledge of glycolytic regulation, if the known cytosol‐located activities of the glycolysis enzymes are taken into account.
